title: Relationship between categorical variables
text:
The data I’m using is the art collection data set from the TidyTuesday GitHub repository . We are investigating if medium is related to thumbnail copyright status. My hypothesis is that it will because the way the artwork is protected depends on the type of art. Whether the artwork is hand-drawn or made with a computer, the copyright policies will be different. So, I expect that the medium will be related to thumbnail copyright status. To test this, I will be developing a statistical analysis plan to see if my hypothesis is true.



The research aim is to investigate whether the type of medium is related to thumbnail copyright status. This will mean we are looking for patterns between medium and thumbnail copyright status. For example, one thumbnail status may be more common for one medium than another. Mediums include the type of art (hand-drawn, painted etc). We will need to see whether certain mediums are more common within different thumbnail copyright status. This way, we will know if they are related.



The variables we will be using are medium and thumbnailCopyright. They are both qualitative variables. This means that they are non-numeric. They are just worded/descriptive data. So, they are slightly harder to work with as they can’t be measured numerically but it’s still possible.



The data preparation we will need is filtering out the missing values from each column. Both columns will likely have missing data, so we need to make sure that these are filtered out for our analysis. This will ensure the results are accurate and not misleading due to poor data. We may also need to clean data entry errors. Poor data collection methods, or human error could lead to data being entered wrong, which can lead to inaccurate results. The data may also need changing so we have frequency counts. Since the data is just qualitative, we may need to transform it so it can be quantified in some way for analysis.



The test that I will be conducting is a chi-square test. This is because we are working with categorical data. More specifically, we will run a chi-square test of independence. This is where you see whether observed frequencies differ from expected frequencies. This method will work best because we are seeing how the different mediums are distributed across different thumbnail copyright status. We will be able to see which status has the most of a specific medium to see if they are related. We are doing a chi-square independence test because it involves two categorical variables, rather than one, like in the goodness-of-fit test. We aren’t using a t-test or ANOVA test because we don’t have measurable data. The only data we can use is categorical data that we need to convert into counts. This way, we can run the chi-square test more effectively and we meet the assumptions.



The assumptions of the chi-square test are the data must be in the form of counts. This means the data we are working with must represent counts or frequencies. The data must also be categorical data. This is data that can be divided into groups. Another assumption is that observations must be independent. This means that the data we are using is unrelated and you can’t use one value to predict another accurately. Another assumption is that cells in the contingency table must be mutually exclusive. This means that each value can only belong to one cell. For example, if you are comparing gender and whether or not they went to university, an individual cannot be both male and female. The final assumption is that the expected frequency of each cell in the contingency table must be at least 5 in 80% of the cells. No cell should have an expected frequency of less than one.



We need ways to make sure that the assumptions of our tests are met. To make sure our data represents counts, we need to check the data. Is it counts/frequencies or is another data type? If it can be transformed into counts, transform it, if not, the chi-square test isn’t suitable. To test if the data is categorical, we again need to check the data itself and make sure it can be sorted in groups. We can also use the isfactor() function in R. If it produces TRUE, then it’s categorical, and FALSE means it is not categorical. This is the easiest way to check. For mutually exclusive observations, you would again analyse the data to make sure that all data is mutually exclusive. For sufficient expected cell counts, we can compute counts using a formula which divides the row total and column total combined with grand total to get an estimated count. If one value is less than one, then the assumptions aren’t met.



The fallback strategy if the assumptions aren’t met varies. If we don’t have enough data, we just need to collect more data so we have enough or do a fishers exact test which specialises in smaller samples. For no independence of data, we can use fisher’s exact test, which is used to determine whether there is a significant association between categorical variables. If the data isn’t categorical, we can instead use t-test or ANOVA if its instead continuous data. These tests are designed for numerical data, whereas chi-square was made specifically to analyse categorical data. If the data isn’t mutually exclusive, the data can be recollected or corrected when doing the test.



For the chi-square test of independence, you will be reporting the contingency table, degrees of freedom and the p-value. When doing an analysis report, having these values/figures will allow you to convey your findings accurately and others will know if there is any significance.
For interpretation, you will be interpreting whether variables are associated or not. If there is, how stable is this association?. Doing this will let you see if your alternative hypothesis is true or not. If the association is weak and has many issues, then you fail to reject the null hypothesis.

title: Group comparison
text:
The data I’m working with is the art collection data set. This is from the TidyTuesday Github Repository. It contains information on artworks, artists, dates, physical dimensions, acquisition details and online metadata. The main question I’m answering is “does artwork width differ according to thumbnail copyright status?”. We are seeing if there are significant changes with artwork width and thumbnail copyright status. One copyright status may favor wider artwork, whereas another may favor shorter art. My main hypothesis is that it may differ slightly as some thumbnail copyright status may prefer certain widths for policy and legal reasons. To see if my hypothesis is true, I will conduct a statistical analysis plan. I will plan out how I will do a statistical analysis on the data, deciding which variables to use, how to prepare it and what model to use to analyse it.



The aim of this research is to investigate whether artwork width will differ according to thumbnail copyright status. So, we will need to find patterns on width changing according to thumbnail copyright status. We can compare different widths for different thumbnail copyright status, and see if there is a pattern, or any significant difference between them. For example, the thumbnail copyright status “@Alex Katz” may have an average artwork width of 400, whereas “@Gerhard Richter” may be 200. There may be a small difference (50 - 100) however, comparing thumbnail copyright statuses will let us spot patterns to answer our question.



The variables that will be needed are width and thumbnail copyright. Width is numerical/continuous data, while thumbnail copyright is categorical data. This is all we need, as we are just focusing on width, rather than other aspects of the art like height or depth, and we are directly comparing thumbnail copyright status’s with width.



The data we have isn’t fully filled in. So, we need to fix the data before we can analyse it. For some rows, data for width and thumbnail copyright are missing. So, we would need to transform these rows before we can analyse the data or conduct tests on it. We can transform it by making the missing data become the average of all widths. This way, we will get a more accurate answer, as missing data can affect means, standard deviation and more, so this is needed. More data preparation that may be needed is to remove outliers that are likely data entry errors. This can affect our analysis and produce the wrong conclusion, if there are enough data entry errors. Also, thumbnailCopyright may need to be transformed into simpler categories or limited to a few when doing the test. There are likely too many unique values, so reducing the nymber of categories may help with the analysis. There may also be unbalanced sample sizes. For example, we may have a large amount of data for one copyright status but a small amount for another. So filtering the data so we have equal/similar sample sizes will help with a more accurate analysis.



The method I would use is a one-way ANOVA test. An ANOVA test will determine if there is a difference between means of two or more groups. A two-way ANOVA test won’t work as it relies on two or more independent variables, whereas we are working with one (thumbnailCopyright) So, a one-way ANOVA will be most appropriate for the number of categories we are working with. Also, ANOVA is used to compare means between categories. Working out the mean for each copyright status will be useful to see any differences, so ANOVA is the most appropriate for our question. The reason why I wouldn’t use a t-test for this, even though these tests are similar, is because a t-test only compares the means of 2 groups. Where as we have more than 2 groups in thumbnailCopyright, so we would need to conduct multiple t-tests. However, doing too many can produce a type I error. This makes the results unrelated. So, an ANOVA test will ensure we are testing all groups and get accurate results, rather than risking getting a type I error.



Assumptions for ANOVA are normal distributions of residuals (difference between observed and predicted values), equal variance across observations and observations are independent from each other. These are assumptions that are made for all tests conducted with ANOVA. A normal distribution of residuals means that the distribution is symmetric around the mean. So, the residuals should produce a bell-shaped curve. This is also known as the Gaussian distribution. This is so our p-value is accurate, which will lead to the right conclusion of the test. Equal variance across groups means that two or more values have similar variance/spread. We assume this because unequal variance will lead to inaccurate p-values which will then lead to an incorrect conclusion. Observations being independent from each other means that the observations have no correlation with each other. ## Diagnostics and model checks
We need to make sure that the assumptions we need for the ANOVA test are met. We do this through diagnostics and model checks. To test normality we can plot a histogram. It should create a bell shape with each bar. This means the center is the tallest one and each bar on the left and right gets smaller. It doesn’t need to be a perfect bell shape but it should resemble one. To test equal variance we could do a side-by-side box plot. This way we can compare the variance across each cell visually. If the variance is similar, then this assumption is met and we can do the ANOVA test. To test variable independence, it’s mostly done by observations of your data. For example, you can produce a residual plot to see if the data points are scattered randomly. If they have a non-random pattern, then it may suggest the variables aren’t independent.



If the diagnostic and model checks show problems, there are a few fallback models we can use instead. For example, if the variance is unequal, we can instead conduct a Welch ANOVA test, as it doesn’t make the assumption of equal variance and is more robust. It adjusts it’s calculations according to the variance so it doesn’t need to assume equal variance. If the distribution is very distorted, then you can try and clean the data again in case there are any data entry errors and that all data types are consistent. You could also use a different statistical method like Bootstrap ANOVA. This version was designed to be a fallback model when the data isn’t normally distributed. If independence in variables is found false, then we can use a mixed model solution instead. This model will account for data dependencies. It’s best used for grouped data, which is what the data set we are working with is. Each thumbnail copyright status is a group with different artwork widths within those groups.



When reporting the one-way ANOVA test, you will be reporting the f-statistic, degrees of freedom and the p-value. These will let you present the test’s results. These are the values we are getting from doing the test, so reporting them will let others know your findings. Your p-value can be the most important as it tells you if the analysis was significant or not.
For interpretation, you will be interpreting whether thumbnail copyright status had an effect on your sample and if there are any patterns. If there is, you will know if your alternative hypothesis is correct.

title: Continuous outcome and multiple explanatory variable
text:
I’m using the data set artwork collection from the TidyTuesday GitHub repository. I’m investigating whether artwork width can be explained by multiple variables. My hypothesis is that it might do. This is because art can be influenced by various things due to legal reasons and how dimensions can affect size. I will see if this is correct by doing a statistical analysis and making a statistical analysis plan.



The research aim is to investigate how artwork width may be explained by a combination of temporal, dimensional and copyright related variables. We will need to see relationships and patterns with these variables and width. We will need to analyse them jointly rather than individually as the investigation requires the combination of these variables. We will need to find a way to compare all of these variables with artwork width to see if they have any correlation or form any kind of pattern.



The variables that will be used are width, year, height and thumbnailCopyright. Width, year and height are continuous numerical data and thumbnailCopyright is categorical. We are working with several variables for this investigation, however their data types are relatively consistent so they may be easy to work with.



The preparation that will be needed for the data is transforming missing values in each column, to prevent misleading results. We would transform it by making all numerical data be equal to the average and make missing thumbnail copyright be equal to no copyright. We will also need to clean/filter data input errors. This may lead to biased results. For the year column, there is a column before it with long text that can go into the year column. This will lead to misleading results and error when doing the test because there will be two different data types in one column. This goes for all columns that may have overlaps with other columns. ThumbnailCopyright will also need converting to dummy variables as some regression models don’t work with text categories.



The proposed method will be multiple linear regression. I have chosen this because it will help with explanation, rather than finding two means like a t-test. Since we have multiple independent variables, we cannot do simple linear regression, we need multiple linear regression. We also cant use a t-test because we have more than two groups. A t-test compare two group means, and we are working with three variables (excluding artwork width) which all have more than two groups. So, we would have to do multiple t-tests and that can cause a type l error. Also, its not all numerical data, so it wouldn’t work. We aren’t using a chi-square test because we have mostly numerical data.



The assumptions for this model are the same as the simple linear regression. Variance of error is equal, independence must be there for all observations, the data follows a normal distribution and the data is linear.



To check the assumptions are correct, a residual plot can be used. This will be used to test linearity and equal variance. This is because a residual plot will show you if errors are consistent and if your data has equal/consistent variance. For normal distribution, a histogram can be used to assess whether the data produces a bell shape with the bars. Then, Independence can be checked by assessing the data collection methods to make sure other variables aren’t involved. ## Fallback strategy
If these assumptions aren’t met, you can use different models/tests depending on what failed. If linearity failed, you can use a non-linear regression model, which is similar to normal regression but doesn’t require linear data. If its independence that failed, you can use auto regression, as it investigates if the current value can be explained by the previous values. If variance and normality fails, you can do a log transformation, which condenses larger values and spreads out smaller ones. This helps stabilise how data is spread.



For reporting, you will report overall model fit, p-values and regression coefficients. These will show if the variables you are using can explain a dependent variable. So, reporting them in a analysis report will help you present results and help decide what to do next.

title: Continuous outcome and one explanatory variable
text:
The data I’m using is the artcollection data-set from the TidyTuesday GitHub repository. I’m investigating whether year of creation will help explain variation in artwork width. My hypothesis is that it will. Art can vary from year to year. Different trends happen in different years. For example, fashion changes every year. Some fashion comes back for a bit, then new fashion designs come out etc. I think this is the same for art. Different styles will become more popular in different years, so year of creation can help explain variation in width. To see if my hypothesis is correct, I will conduct a statistical analysis on it and develop a SAP (statistical analysis plan)



The research aim is to investigate whether year of creation helps explain variation in artwork width. We will need to find patterns and relationships between width and year of creation. For example, we may find a pattern/relationship that shows artwork in 2014, 2016 and 2019 has larger artwork widths, where as years like 2015, 2017 may have produced narrower artwork.



The variables that will be used are year and width. These are both continuous numerical. Knowing the data types you are working with will help you determine your test without meaningfully analysing it. Some tests are made for specific data types. So, knowing how to identify them is important.



Data preparation we may need is cleaning the data. For example, the column before year has longer words, so these go into the year column, which can ruin the data by having two different data types in one column. It would also make the data incorrect and lead to inaccurate results. This will be done for all columns. We also need to transform empty rows for both variables. Some data may be missing, so to make the results be as accurate as possible, transforming the missing data into the average of all other values will make sure we aren’t filtering data while still making sure we get accurate results.



The proposed method will be doing is linear regression. Linear regression models the relationship between a single explanatory variable and an outcome variable. For this question, the explanatory variable is the year of creation, and the outcome variable is the width. With this, we can see if there is a relationship between the different years of creation. This test is the most appropriate because we are investigating a relationship between years and width. A chi-square test isn’t appropriate because we don’t have categorical values. We can’t use a t-test because that compares means of 2 groups. While it is possible, we would need to do multiple t-tests because there are more than one groups, and conducting multiple t-tests can lead to errors. So, a linear regression model best suits our needs and other models wouldn’t work due to data types and what we want from the test. The specific test that I would do is a simple linear regression test, as we are only working with one independent variable (year). A multiple linear regression test isn’t suitable because we only have one predictor variable. We could use multiple linear regression if we were seeing if year AND medium affected width but since we only have year, simple linear regression is enough.



The assumptions of this test are linearity, independence, normality and equal variance. Linearity means the relationship between variables follows a straight-line pattern. If the data is curved, the line of best fit wont work as its a linear line. Independence means each observation is independent from each other. This means knowing the value of one observation shouldn’t allow you to accurately predict the other. Normality is when the residuals produce a bell-shaped curve. Residuals is the difference between predicted and observed values. Equal variance means all residuals are spread out consistently.



To check that our assumptions are correct, we can use a residual plot for linearity and equal variance. This is because a residual plot will plot the differences between predicted and observed values. This will let us assess whether the relationship between the data is linear. It will also let us see if we have equal variance as we can see each error and decide if they are equal/similar. For normality, we can use a histogram to see if the bars produce a bell shape when plotting errors Then for independence we can analyse how the data was collected to make sure all variables were independent.



If the diagnostic checks fail, then we need a fallback strategy. If linearity fails, then we can use non-linear regression. This is linear regression but instead the data doesn’t need to be linear. If independence fails, then we can use auto regression. This a model that uses data where the current value can be explained by previous values. This allows for correlated data to be tested. If variance fails, we can transform the data by doing log transformations. This will condense large values and spread out smaller ones. This will help with stabilising variance. if normality fails, we can again transform the variables with log transformations.



For reporting, you will report regression coefficients, the intercept, f-statistic and p-value. These are results you get from using the model and tests within it. These will allow you to present your findings and can provide more details rather than just saying variables can explain something.
For interpretation, you will see whether the predictor can predict outcomes well and with accuracy, direction of the relationship between variables. These will show if there is a significant pattern that can be used to show a variable can explain something.
